highlights.title: Opaque recurrence, and other AI terms that you should probably know
highlights.summary: The rise of AI has brought an avalanche of new terms and slang. Here is a glossary with definitions of some of the most important words and phrases you might encounter.
body: AI is rewriting the world and, at the same time, inventing a whole new language to describe how it’s doing it. Sit in on any product meeting, pitch, or panel these days, and you’ll hear people toss around LLMs, RAG, RLHF — and, as of last week, terms like “opaque recurrence,” the reasoning technique in OpenAI’s new Astra model that’s got AI safety researchers rattled. The vocabulary moves fast enough to make even very smart people in the tech world feel a little insecure.

This glossary is our attempt to fix that: plain-English definitions of the AI terms you’re most likely to see, whether you’re building with this stuff, investing in it, or just trying to keep up by reading TechCrunch or listening to related podcasts. We update it regularly as the field evolves, so consider it a living document, much like the AI systems it describes.

The GTA series is often divided into three eras: the "2D universe," the "3D universe," and the "HD universe." As a broad rule of thumb, the games in the 3D and HD universes are mostly available, with some caveats, while the 2D universe games are unavailable unless you have old hardware or are prepared to get creative.
Now let's run down every game in the series and where you can play it.

highlights.title: Audi’s new A2 E-tron is its most affordable and efficient EV yet
highlights.summary: When shopping for an electric vehicle, affordability is becoming a more common trait. But affordable and energy efficient is truly a rare breed. Often you have to sacrifice one for the other. Want something affordable? Great, here's a range loser. Want something that goes the distance?
body: Unfortunately it won’t be making it’s way to North America any time soon.

Surprisingly, here comes Audi to split the difference. The German automaker’s new A2 E-tron compact crossover is inexpensive, starting at just £32,200 (about $45,000). And it absolutely impresses with an ultra low drag coefficient and a range of battery and drivetrain options that, when configured correctly, can produce a range of up to 401 miles.

Unfortunately for us Yanks, this rear-wheel drive compact car is just for the European market for now. But perhaps Audi will eventually see the error of its ways, or Americans will get their heads out of their tailpipes long enough to see the real advantages of a highly efficient, compact EV with an Audi badge.

Efficient is often synonymous with aerodynamic, and the A2 E-tron certainly confirms that. Flush door handles, cool air intakes, a fully enclosed underbody, and gap reducers around the wheel arches help reduce the drag coefficient down to 0.24, a first for Audi. Another first is bidirectional charging, which will help support vehicle-t0-load via an outlet in the trunk, or vehicle-to-home with the right compatible DC wall box.
points: When shopping for an electric vehicle, affordability is becoming a more common trait.
But affordable and energy efficient is truly a rare breed.
The German automaker’s new A2 E-tron compact crossover is inexpensive, starting at just £32,200 (about $45,000).

highlights.title: Whispering Complaints Into Your Phone May Be the Future of Customer Feedback
highlights.summary: Forget email surveys or long calls spent on hold. Voicebox lets people send customer feedback by recording a voice note on their phone.
body: Some of the hottest software this year revolves around capturing voices. Whether it’s the sharp dictations of Wispr or the always-listening ears of Granola, voice-centered software currently feels inescapable. Voice dictation is getting so sharp, in fact, that I often write drafts in my notepad and then dictate aloud to my laptop.

Some prognosticators have declared this to be a dramatic end-of-the-keyboard moment, where legions of white-collar workers will soon be quietly whispering into desk microphones rather than clacking away at keyboards. I disagree, but I do think these changes could upend how customers give feedback.

I rarely email customer support unless something substantially negative has happened and I’m fishing for a refund. I’m much more open to giving feedback by blabbering for 20 seconds into my phone, good or bad, than I am to waiting on hold for who knows how long until someone answers.

body: The winning combination of whimsy, gravitas and good looks that Gael García Bernal has brought to both the big ( Amores Perros, Y tu mamá tambíen ) and small ( Mozart in the Jungle ) screens fails to translate to his second stab as director, Hombre Al Agua, an offbeat dramedy that’s too chaotic and muddled to hit its marks.

The actor-director tosses all he can at his protagonist without much logic, in what feels like a rudderless midlife crisis scenario that never finds a strong throughline. highlights.title: A health MOT is just one step towards prevention | Letters
highlights.summary: Tackling social and economic conditions must come first, writes Dr Louise Lawson. Plus letters from James Hibberd, Bob Forster and Dr Giles Youngs. Devi Sridhar is right to welcome free cholesterol testing on the NHS in England and blood pressure checks in pharmacies.
body: Sridhar’s proposed five-point health MOT is undoubtedly valuable, but it is better understood as identifying risk rather than preventing disease. Prevention is what comes next: enabling people to make changes that improve health and reduce that risk. Public health has long distinguished between upstream factors, such as poverty, housing, employment, access to affordable healthy food and safe green spaces, and downstream interventions focused on individuals. Screening and health checks sit much closer to the downstream end of that spectrum.

Interventions aimed at changing behaviour emphasise individual responsibility and often assume that everyone has similar economic, social and psychological resources to adopt healthier lifestyles. Yet those living on low incomes, in insecure work or facing linguistic and cultural barriers often have far less capacity to act on health advice. Such approaches can also reinforce stigma by implying that poor health results primarily from individual choices rather than the circumstances in which people live, while diverting attention from the drivers of health inequalities.
points: Tackling social and economic conditions must come first, writes Dr Louise Lawson.
Plus letters from James Hibberd, Bob Forster and Dr Giles Youngs.

highlights.title: The Best Kitchen Composter Actually Makes Compost With No Stench or Mess
highlights.summary: Electric composting machines and food recyclers promise to turn food scraps into grounds with zero stench and minimal cleanup. Here are the ones we recommend.
body: I consider myself a fairly eco-conscious person. I reduce, reuse, recycle; I take public transit; I avoid using AI for meme-making and learning celebrity heights. But composting never really took. I'd try to gather food scraps in a plastic countertop compost bin in my kitchen, but emptying and cleaning the receptacle every couple days was messy and smelly and I'd give up after a couple weeks. In 2025, however, New York City made composting the law of the land and I knew I needed to figure out a more sustainable solution.

Electric kitchen composters and food recyclers promise to turn your food scraps into dried grounds or usable compost in a matter of hours, eliminating the need to transport a dripping bag of rotting food goo through your apartment and around the block to where your building keeps the communal bin (just me?). Like magic, these machines can reduce the volume of your food waste by up to 90%, so you can go weeks or months without emptying them. The downside? Many of them are very expensive.

In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Fermat’s last theorem, one of the most celebrated mathematical results of the last half-century, has been turned into computer-verified code for the first time, using an advanced prototype of the artificial-intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude.

The fact that a machine could turn the work of human mathematicians into a 13-million-line-long, ironclad proof “just completely blew my mind”, says Alex Kontorovich, a number theorist at Rutgers University in Piscataway, New Jersey. Claude-maker Anthropic AI, of San Francisco, California, announced the breakthrough on 4 September. The model finished in 11 days a project that was expected to take humans 10 years.

highlights.summary: New York Times bestselling author Aiden Thomas captured hearts and minds with the debut of Cemetery Boys in September 2020. It wasn't hard to see why: Cemetery Boys is a blissfully queer coming-of-age urban fantasy story that wrestles with identity, love, and finding your place in a community.
body: Moreover, its characters, Yadriel and Julian, were deliciously complicated. Yadriel, desperate to prove himself a real brujo and free the ghost of his murdered cousin, accidentally ends up summoning Julian instead. With Julian also determined to find out the cause of his death, the two boys have no choice but to team up — only to discover complicated feelings along the way.

Cemetery Boys: Espíritu picks up shortly after the original novel's ending. This time, readers follow Julian, who has a big problem: he can't stop seeing dark spots on people. Julian has no idea what these spots mean, and even Yadriel and his community are stumped. Answers start to come to light only when Angel, a nonbinary brujx who sees the same spots as Julian, shows up.

With Espíritu set to release today, Polygon got a sneak peek at one of the later chapters of the urban fantasy, narrated by Puerto Rican actor, drag king, and Critical Role newcomer, Vico Ortiz. highlights.title: ‘No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman’ Review: Iraq’s Oscar Submission Offers a Patriotic Anthem to the Kurdish Peshmerga’s Fight Against Islamic State
highlights.summary: The trope of the lone action hero with near-superhuman strength gets a gender switch in “No Paradise If You Are Killed By A Woman,” a visually impressive drama about a resourceful female Peshmerga sniper.
body: A female Kurdish sniper searches Mosul for her sister who was kidnapped by Islamic State in Norwegian-Kurdish director Halkawt Mustafa's out-of-competition Venice premiere.

As Vyan’s poetic voiceover narration states, Peshmerga means “before death” and its fighters enter combat out of strength, not out of fear. Certainly, Vyan is fearless. She reckons that she has killed more than 100 of the enemy in three years. Given that, as the title notes, IS fighters believe that there is “No Paradise If You Are Killed by A Woman,” it’s no wonder they have placed a million-dollar bounty on her head.

The last half of the film feels as if it could easily be adapted into a tense video game as it follows Vyan silently creeping through tunnels and crawling through the aftermath of IS carnage. It certainly gives a more detailed picture of how a sniper operates, and the lonely patience required for the job, than Clint Eastwood’s “American Sniper” ever did. Vyan uses logic and the help of friendly Kurdish commander from the Iraqi government forces in Mosul to locate the IS snipers preventing civilians from leaving the devastated city.

highlights.title: My favorite family heirloom: an old Zojirushi hot water dispenser better than any tea kettle
highlights.summary: It heats water up fast and crucially, keeps it warm for the whole day, so you can can access hot water to your heart’s content. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: O f all the things my mother has given me from the vast warehouse of her garage, there are two items I treasure the most. One, a Costco-sized box of gallon-sized Ziploc bags, and two, a battered Zojirushi water boiler that has been in the family for decades. The Ziploc bags are nice to have and can be easily replaced; the water boiler, on the other hand, has become an indispensable tool that makes my life at home a little better, every time I use it.

A brief twist: if given the choice, I’d take an ice cold beverage over hot any time. But even I, with my preference for drinks so cold that they hurt my teeth, have been converted to my family’s beloved Zojirushi.

I use it almost every day – for the instant Cafe Bustelo coffee that I drink every morning, for instant noodles, for tea and hot chocolate and any other wintry weather beverage. Once you’ve opened your heart (and wallet) to one of these things, I promise you that you will never look back.

highlights.title: Six years later, Sony revisits its legendary XM4 headphones
highlights.summary: Six years ago Sony and Bose were in the middle of a noise-canceling battle, with each new model of headphones better than the last. In the fall of 2020, Sony released the WH-1000XM4 headphones to wide acclaim.
body: After the WH-1000XM4 were discontinued in 2025, Sony is bringing them back as the WH-1000XM4C.

The XM4C look identical to the original XM4 (although they now have a lavender option), with the same hinge design and ability to fold up. It’s a compact design that Sony moved away from when it released the XM5 in 2022, and then returned to (although not quite as compact) with the XM6. But it’s not just the look that’s returned. The XM4C still use the same QN1 processing chip and four microphones for ANC. That design is showing its age: The XM5 still used the QN1, but had eight mics. Last year’s XM6 have 12, plus the new QN3 chip.

Sony did update the XM4C’s sound profile to bring it in line with current models, and the headphones have a 10-band EQ in the Headphones app, instead of the 5-band on the XM4, plus a gaming preset. The XM4C also support Bluetooth 6 instead of 5. Surprisingly, the battery performance on the new headphones is slightly worse. Sony claims the XM4C get up to 27 hours of use with ANC on as opposed to 30 hours previously. Not a huge difference, and still more than enough for a cross-country trip.

highlights.title: ‘Mistrust’ of Palantir may affect NHS research, says health minister
highlights.summary: James Frith says patients may be less willing to share data as new figures show a rise in opt-outs. Concern is being raised about Palantir’s work with the NHS as new figures showed tens of thousands of patients have withdrawn their data from use in research projects.
body: James Frith, the health innovation minister, said he was worried about “mistrust” of the US defence and health tech company and “the impact it could have on people’s willingness to share data with the NHS”.
The government is deciding whether to axe the company’s £330m contract to operate the health service’s federated data platform, which is intended to improve efficiency and patient outcomes.

Frith’s comment, in a letter to Layla Moran, the chair of the Commons health committee, follows a rise in patients opting out of allowing their medical data to be shared. In the two months from mid-May to mid-July, 60,000 more people withdrew their private information under a mechanism called the national data opt-out.

Doctors and patients’ groups are calling for Labour to exercise a break clause in Palantir’s seven-year contract. They cite its work with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s ICE immigration agency and question the company’s claim to provide value for money.

highlights.title: Persona 1 and 2 remakes are "something we'll probably eventually do," series producer says
highlights.summary: With Persona 3 Reload out the door and Persona 4 Revival next in line, series producer Kazuhisa Wada has said remakes of the first two games will "probably" happen as well.
body: Developer Atlus seems to be on a mission to revisit every high-schooling, demon-mashing, double-life-simulating game it's ever made. In 2024, the studio pulled the gun on Persona 3 Reload before starting work on Persona 4 Revival, coming next February. But Atlus may reach even further back for some new (old) source material.

In an interview with RPS, Wada said the team originally came up with the idea to remake Persona 3 and Persona 4 around the same time. The latter "had to be put" on the backburner for a while, but the intent for both was the same. "I think a remaster or remake is some kind of cultural preservation," he said, per a translator.

Wada continued to explain that it's Atlus' "duty" to make sure its older games aren't lost to time "and are still around in the modern day." With that in mind, "Persona 1 and 2 are something we'll probably eventually do, too." There you have it, folks.

Persona 1 and Persona 2 are also the only mainline games in the series that aren't readily available to buy on any modern system, making Wada's point about "cultural preservation" even more salient here.

Not you -- even though you bought it -- but them. They also talk about knowing everybody in the household, knowing the secondary devices, moving from TVs to smartphones and other screens, and more in their B2B discussions. Beyond just the fact that we think the TV's native behavior parallels malware, the LG Smart TVs we tested also have a number of security vulnerabilities that can be exploited to convert the TVs into covert listening devices. In this investigation, we dive into the mix of LG's first-party functionality that (in our opinions) is tantamount to spying and LG's vulnerabilities and exploits that they have failed to protect against.
